Female Corn snakes emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that, when maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], lasts approximately 70 days [ab = approximately 70 days]. This developmental duration, measured in captive incubation trials, is somewhat protracted compared to some other North American colubrids and is tightly linked to thermal conditions during embryogenesis. Hatchling females, upon eclosion, exhibit a total body length averaging 30.5 cm [Lb = 30.5 cm], a size that positions them well for immediate post-hatching foraging on small lizards and neonate rodents. The corresponding wet mass at birth for a typical female neonate is 7.5 grams [Wwb = 7.5 grams]. This initial mass is modest relative to the considerable size the species will eventually attain, reflecting the altricial-like state of the hatchling despite its precocial capacity for independent feeding. The energetic investment per offspring, largely tied to yolk provisioning within the leathery-shelled egg, appears calibrated to produce a relatively large and robust neonate capable of exploiting a wide prey size spectrum from the moment of hatching, a strategy common among medium-sized constrictors.

As juveniles grow, they undergo a period of rapid somatic expansion before reaching reproductive competence. Under controlled laboratory conditions held at a steady 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty, or the interval required for a female to attain gonadal maturation, is approximately 600 days [tp = approximately 600 days]. This duration reflects the necessity of accumulating sufficient body reserves and achieving a minimum size threshold before the onset of vitellogenesis and the capacity to produce a viable first clutch. Field-caught individuals from wild populations in the southeastern United States may exhibit slightly more variable maturation timelines due to seasonal fluctuations in prey availability and thermal regimes, but the captive data provide a robust baseline. During this juvenile phase, growth is characterized by steady increases in both length and mass, and the snake transitions through a series of skin sheds. The attainment of puberty marks a critical life-history transition, shifting energetic allocation from primarily somatic growth toward the demanding processes of gametogenesis and, eventually, reproductive activity.

Upon reaching adulthood, female Corn snakes demonstrate considerable reproductive potential under optimal thermal and nutritional conditions. When housed at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], which approximates the thermal optimum for many physiological processes in this species, females produce an average of 12 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 12 eggs per clutch] and are capable of depositing 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year]. This level of output constitutes the maximum reproductive rate observed for the species under controlled conditions. The eggs are elongated, leathery-shelled, and are typically laid in a concealed, humid retreat such as a rotting log or rodent burrow. Clutch size can vary with female body size and condition, with larger, more robust females often producing the maximum number of ova. The ability to generate two discrete clutches within a single active season allows Corn snakes to capitalize on long favorable periods, a reproductive strategy that enhances annual fecundity considerably when compared with species that produce only a single, larger clutch annually.

The ultimate total length attained by a mature female Pantherophis guttatus is substantial, with maximum recorded specimens reaching approximately 182 cm [Li = approximately 182 cm]. This impressive length places the Corn snake among the larger-bodied members of its genus, with females routinely exceeding males in overall size, a common pattern in colubrid snakes where fecundity selection favors larger female body volume. Correlated with this considerable skeletal dimension is the corresponding ultimate wet weight, which reaches up to 1642 grams [Wwi = up to 1642 grams] in the largest, most robust individuals. This mass is achieved after several years of growth and reflects the accumulation of both skeletal muscle and substantial fat reserves, which are critical for surviving periods of winter brumation and for fueling the energetic demands of oogenesis. Comparisons with congeners such as Pantherophis obsoletus suggest that the growth trajectory of Corn snakes is slightly slower, but the ultimate body sizes are within a similar range, underscoring a shared life-history strategy of reaching large body size to maximize reproductive output.

Longevity is another key feature of the Corn snake's life history, particularly under captive conditions where predation and environmental stressors are minimized. Records from zoological institutions indicate that individuals can live for approximately 32.3 years [am = approximately 32.3 years] when maintained at a thermal regime centered on 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This age-related death typically occurs after a prolonged period of reproductive senescence, during which fecundity and egg viability decline. In the wild, maximum lifespan is likely considerably shorter due to predation from raptors, mammals, and larger snakes, as well as habitat pressures. Nonetheless, the physiological capacity for such an extended life, combined with the attainment of puberty at roughly 600 days [tp = roughly 600 days], illustrates a life-history pattern that prioritizes a long reproductive window over a short, intense burst of at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]breeding. This strategy is consistent with a species that inhabits relatively stable, though seasonal, environments where annual mortality is moderate and the benefits of iteroparity are pronounced.
